scope: Read-only native browser TLS1.3 resumption investigation against the owned public site, normal HTTPS trust, end-to-end TLS through a loopback proxy, no server/system/trust changes. No ticket identities, binders, keys, session secrets or certificate contents retained.
conclusion: Public Chromium TLS1.3 PSK resumption is observed on the second and third connections. WebKit 26.6 offers no PSK in tested follow-up connections, including after a natural 73.3-second server idle close, with persistent context, and without request interception. Its ClientHello does advertise PSK key-exchange modes. WebKit empty-nonce resumption compatibility remains unestablished.
limits: The observed ClientHello contains no PSK identity offer; this cannot distinguish ticket-content rejection from retention, proxy or platform policy.
Public production currently uses the compact nonce. No otherwise identical ordinary-trust eight-byte-nonce public control was deployed for this investigation.
Earlier self-signed WebKit controls did not resume either nonce variant and therefore do not establish ordinary-trust baseline behavior.
TLS1.3 NewSessionTicket is encrypted. The proxy does not inspect ticket contents or independently identify its nonce.
Forced TCP half-close controls are paired with a natural server idle closure to avoid interpreting a premature close as ticket rejection.
worthwhileNextChecks: Keep a PSK capability/offer/selection distinction in future browser regressions, including fragmented Hello parsing and no-secret-report checks.

For a decisive WebKit nonce comparison, use otherwise identical ordinary-trust endpoints with eight-byte, empty and optionally one-byte first nonces; do not substitute successful page rendering for observed resumption.
A one-byte first nonce would retain seven of eight saved bytes while avoiding the empty-vector edge case, but it also needs ordinary-trust WebKit evidence before compatibility claims.
